classification.difficultyReason: Recall definitions, vertical-line-test conditions and function notation using sentence cues and supplied initial letters. No linked calculation or unfamiliar interpretation is required.

questions.mappingNote: The eight assigned clozes directly assess the definitions named in their prompts. The supplied F1 body provides local context.
questions.methodNote: Recall the definitions of relation and function, apply the vertical line test and interpret function notation and piecewise definitions. Separate teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the one-output-per-input definition to finite ordered-pair sets and variable families, distinguishing repeated outputs from repeated inputs and interpreting fixed-coordinate cases.

questions.mappingNote: All four items present ordered pairs or ordered-pair families, so the definition of a function directly determines each classification.
questions.methodNote: Test whether each input has exactly one output, as recalled in the supplied F1(b)–(c). Separate teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the vertical line test to supplied graphs, distinguishing repeated intersections from single outputs. The hardest decisions are interpreting the open and closed endpoints in (i) and recognising that the excluded input in (j) does not prevent the graph representing a function.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve assigned graphs share the instruction on page 2. Endpoint inclusion in part (i), restricted domain in part (j), and repeated intersections in parts (d), (g) and (l) are assessed through that test.
questions.methodNote: Apply the vertical line test recalled in the supplied F1(d)–(f). Separate teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly substitute 2 into each supplied rule and simplify using powers, a square root and a fraction.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess numerical evaluation in function notation.
questions.methodNote: Substitute 2 for x and simplify using order of operations. Teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Replace x by each complete algebraic argument in a linear rule, distribute where needed and combine the reciprocal result into one fraction.

questions.mappingNote: The shared linear rule applies independently to all ten arguments, including radicals and a reciprocal.
questions.methodNote: Replace x in 2x+1 by the complete argument, then simplify. Teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute complete algebraic arguments into a quadratic rule, preserving signs and grouping, then link binomial expansion with distribution and simplification in part d.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts use the shared quadratic rule and directly assess algebraic substitution.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the complete argument in parentheses before squaring, then expand and simplify. Teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute grouped arguments into a reciprocal-square rule, simplify nested reciprocals and a squared radical, and retain the sum as a complete squared denominator.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts share the reciprocal-square rule. The sum in part d remains grouped in the denominator.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the complete argument into the squared denominator and simplify reciprocals and products. Teaching pages were unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate branch for each numerical input, including the boundary value 1, then perform a direct square or subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: The piecewise definition is supplied within Q7. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Select the branch using the input inequality, then substitute and evaluate.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the applicable interval in a three-branch definition; the final part requires evaluating two inputs using different branches and subtracting their outputs.

questions.mappingNote: All branch definitions are embedded in Q8. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Check each input against the three domain conditions before evaluating. Part d uses two branches.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute algebraic arguments into the square function and compare identities using expansion and index laws. The hardest parts require recognising cancelling cross terms or the reciprocal cross term, while distinguishing a false sum identity.

questions.mappingNote: Q9 supplies its own function. Real-domain restrictions are stated in the answers where needed. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Substitute each algebraic argument into the square function and compare the two sides. Use a counterexample for a false identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate each function at k and k-1, preserve subtraction brackets, and select the appropriate simplification procedure: polynomial expansion, a common denominator or factoring a common exponential power.

questions.mappingNote: Each part supplies its own function and shares the difference instruction. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Substitute k and k-1, subtract with brackets, then simplify using expansion, a common denominator or exponent laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute algebraic arguments into an exponential rule and select exponent laws to establish the identities; the hardest part links rewriting a shifted exponent with extracting a common power.

questions.mappingNote: Q11 supplies f(x)=4^x for all three identities. The answer key supplies a worked-solutions pointer. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Substitute into the exponential function, use exponent laws and factor common powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the reciprocal argument to obtain 2x, then divide the two function values by multiplying by the reciprocal and simplify the resulting algebraic fraction.

questions.mappingNote: The reciprocal function and complete task are embedded in Q12. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the function at the reciprocal argument, then divide using the reciprocal of the divisor.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply each supplied recurrence twice from its initial value, carrying f(2) into the calculation of f(3) and using the current index as the multiplier in part b.

questions.mappingNote: Each part supplies a recurrence, an initial value and its applicable index condition. The closest available catalogue skill is function-notation. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Use the initial value to calculate f(2), then use f(2) to calculate f(3).

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the negative argument and apply the product law for powers with the same base; the opposite exponents cancel to give the zero power.

questions.mappingNote: Q14 supplies the exponential function and identity. The answer key supplies a worked-solutions pointer. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Substitute x and -x, then add exponents when multiplying powers with the same base.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute −x into the supplied polynomial, simplify the odd power and factor out −1 to reach the stated identity.

questions.mappingNote: Q15 directly assesses substitution of an algebraic argument into the supplied function and simplification to the requested identity.
questions.methodNote: Substitute -x for x, simplify the odd power, then factor out -1. Teaching pages were not supplied, so the source's taught sequence could not be verified.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the reciprocal argument into a rational rule, simplify the resulting complex fraction and combine two fractions to establish the supplied identity.

questions.mappingNote: The definition and requested identity directly assess substitution of an algebraic argument. Relevant teaching evidence was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the reciprocal argument into the rational rule, simplify the complex fraction, then add over a common denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute 1/x into the rational rule and clear reciprocal powers by multiplying numerator and denominator by x², then recognise the original function.

questions.mappingNote: The reciprocal-argument identity assesses algebraic substitution and rational simplification. Relevant teaching evidence was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the reciprocal argument and multiply the numerator and denominator by x squared.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the rule at two numerical inputs while retaining the parameter, translate the given function relationship into a linear equation and solve for p.

questions.mappingNote: The parameter is determined through evaluations of the supplied quadratic rule. Relevant teaching evidence was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the function at both numerical inputs, substitute into the given condition and solve the resulting linear equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse each supplied input shift or scaling to recover the original function, then simplify quadratic expansions or a compound rational expression. The main decision is expressing the old variable in terms of the complete function input.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and c reverse additive input shifts, part b reverses a subtractive input shift, and part d reverses an input scaling. Relevant teaching evidence was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Name the complete input u, express x in terms of u, substitute into the given right-hand side and simplify before renaming the input x.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the reciprocal argument, clear the compound fraction and recognise that reversing the denominator's terms changes its sign, allowing the two function values to cancel.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded rational definition and reciprocal identity form one independent task. Relevant teaching evidence was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the reciprocal argument, clear the compound fraction and use 1−x²=−(x²−1) before adding.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect the paired sum-and-difference definitions through difference of squares or expansion, then use the product of reciprocal powers to reduce the expression to a constant.

questions.mappingNote: Both exponential definitions are retained together as permanent givens. The closest supplied skill is manipulation of algebraic expressions in function notation; the catalogue has no dedicated function-identity skill. Relevant teaching evidence was not supplied.
questions.methodNote: Factor the difference of squares, substitute the two function definitions and apply the index law for multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the complete rational expression into both occurrences of the function input, clear the internal denominator and simplify parameter expressions to expose a cancellable non-zero factor. The composition and required restrictions are supplied.

questions.mappingNote: The explicit self-composition assesses composite functions. Relevant teaching evidence was not supplied. The original parameter statement requires correction for the identity to be defined.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the complete rational expression into the function rule, clear the internal denominator, expand and cancel the non-zero common parameter factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate directly between inequalities and interval notation by deciding whether each endpoint is included; each part supplies the other representation.

questions.mappingNote: F1(a–d) directly assesses conversion between the two representations; no separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: The embedded interval-completion activity pairs inequalities with open and closed endpoint notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the input variable and the name of the output set within supplied definitions, with an initial-letter cue for range.

questions.mappingNote: F2(a) completes the input variable; F2(b) completes the output-set terminology.
questions.methodNote: The question embeds the definitions of domain as allowed inputs and range as possible outputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply nonzero-denominator and non-negative-radicand rules, then combine them for 1/√x; preceding parts and the explicit zero cue support the final decision.

questions.mappingNote: Each response completes the domain condition for its own displayed function; the second blank in F3(c) retains the printed initial z.
questions.methodNote: The activity progresses from a nonzero denominator to a non-negative radicand, then combines both restrictions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the non-negative ranges of the square and principal square-root functions and complete supplied sign explanations and range terminology.

questions.mappingNote: F4(a–b) complete a range condition and its reason; F4(c) completes the name of the output set.
questions.methodNote: The embedded explanations connect non-negative square and square-root outputs with range.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate supplied inequalities directly into intervals, choosing endpoint brackets and using parentheses at infinity; no inequality solving is required.

questions.mappingNote: Q1 applies this correspondence to numerical endpoints, including unbounded intervals in parts d–f.
questions.methodNote: F1 on the same inspected source page establishes the correspondence between inequality signs and endpoint brackets.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate endpoint brackets into strict or inclusive inequalities and recognise intervals with only one finite bound; no algebraic solving is required.

questions.mappingNote: Q2 reverses the conversion in Q1; each part contains its own complete interval and requires no dependency.
questions.methodNote: F1 on the same inspected source page establishes the correspondence between endpoint brackets and inequality signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Read open and filled endpoints and ray directions from number lines, then express each represented set using interval brackets and infinity.

questions.mappingNote: Each of the six source number lines directly assesses conversion to interval notation. Worked answers use endpoint interpretation without an algebraic substitution.
questions.methodNote: Read filled endpoints as included and open endpoints as excluded; read ray arrows as unbounded sets. Use square brackets for included finite endpoints and parentheses for excluded endpoints and infinity. No teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Read horizontal and vertical extents from supplied graphs, including closed endpoints and attained extrema while excluding asymptotic bounds. The varied curves require direct graphical interpretation without algebraic derivation or an unsignposted connection.

questions.mappingNote: Each labelled source graph maps to its corresponding a–o response leaf. Parts a,c,e have unrestricted extents; b,d have included minima; f,m,n,o have included finite extremes; g has filled finite endpoints and attained extrema; h,i,k exclude asymptotes; j,l include the origin.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Read domain from horizontal extent and range from vertical extent, including attained endpoints and excluding asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Read horizontal and vertical extents from supplied graphs, distinguish included extrema from excluded asymptotes, and express the disconnected domain in part (e) using 'or'.

questions.mappingNote: a: fixed x; b: fixed y; c: both axes excluded; d: both horizontal limits excluded; e: disjoint horizontal extents joined by 'or'; f: maximum included and lower asymptote excluded.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. Read horizontal and vertical extents from the supplied graphs, distinguishing attained values from asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the supplied square-root domain rule, then require each radicand to be nonnegative and solve a simple linear inequality, including upper-bound cases with negative x coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded rule remains in a. The four b leaves apply it respectively to x, x−2, 5−x and 7−2x; source roman labels and two-column order retained.
questions.methodNote: Q6(a) itself supplies the method: require the expression inside the square root to be nonnegative. No separate teaching pages supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the supplied denominator rule, solve simple equations for forbidden inputs, and recognise that an external constant and a squared denominator do not introduce additional exclusions.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded rule remains in a. The b leaves apply it to x, x−1, 2x−3, x+2, x−7 and (x−3)², retaining the external +3 in v and all source roman labels.
questions.methodNote: The method is supplied within Q7(a): set the denominator equal to zero, solve, and exclude those values. No separate teaching pages supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the square-root and nonzero-denominator conditions into a strict inequality, then solve linear inequalities, reversing the sign for the negative coefficient in (d); the stem explicitly cues the two rules.

questions.mappingNote: Four independent denominator-radical domains remain under the source shared instruction.
questions.methodNote: No teaching pages supplied. The stem explicitly combines the methods from Questions 6 and 7; solutions combine square-root existence with a nonzero denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the scaffolded connection between denominator zeros and excluded inputs, then factor quadratic denominators independently; the final part requires retaining an excluded input even when a numerator factor cancels.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) remain together; part (c) retains its nested two-column grid.
questions.methodNote: The question itself supplies the progression: solve a factored equation, exclude denominator zeros, then factor further quadratic denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Obtain software graphs and translate their extrema, disconnected branches and asymptotic behaviour into domains and ranges, distinguishing attained endpoints from excluded asymptotic values.

questions.mappingNote: Four functions retain the source two-column order. All answer graphs remain solution-only.
questions.methodNote: The source explicitly requires graphing software and graphical interpretation. Worked answers describe graph features rather than substituting an algebraic range proof.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect vertex form and a labelled sketch to range, complete the square for two quadratics, then generalise the attained minimum as k; preceding parts scaffold these linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: All dependent parts remain in one selectable question. The four examples in part (d) retain the nested two-column structure.
questions.methodNote: Embedded sequence: read a vertex, sketch and label the parabola, infer its range, complete the square where needed, then generalise.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied nonnegativity of a square to scaled, shifted and reflected quadratics, deciding whether each attained bound is a minimum or maximum.

questions.mappingNote: The reminder remains permanent editable question content. All nine functions retain the source three-column row-major order.
questions.methodNote: The embedded reminder supplies the method: use nonnegativity of a square to identify each attained minimum or maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Transform the supplied nonnegative square-root range by positive scaling, vertical shifts and reflection, choosing the resulting lower or upper bound.

questions.mappingNote: The recall is retained once in the parent prompt. Parts a–f independently assess the ranges of the six printed transformations. No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the embedded recall that the principal square root is nonnegative, then apply the displayed multiplication, sign change or vertical shift.

classification.difficultyReason: Use a quadratic maximum to bound a square-root output, combine it with the nonnegative-radicand restriction and check attained endpoints, then apply the technique to an unbounded radicand.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) establishes the upper bound used explicitly by part (b). Part (c) retains the source instruction to use a similar technique. The embedded recall in Q13 and the progression within Q14 support this method; no separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: First use the non-negativity of x squared to bound the radicand. Then restrict to nonnegative radicand values and take principal square roots, checking attained endpoints.

classification.difficultyReason: Find and intersect the two linear radicand restrictions, then remove the quadratic denominator's zeros, recognising that both initially allowed endpoints must be excluded.

questions.mappingNote: The two radicals and quadratic denominator directly assess simultaneous domain restrictions. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Require each radicand to be nonnegative and the denominator to be nonzero; intersect the restrictions.

classification.difficultyReason: Use software to sketch a rational function with three branches, then recognise from the middle branch that every real output occurs; the graphical method and follow-up are explicitly supplied.

questions.mappingNote: The source explicitly requests a graphical method and makes part (b) depend on the graph in part (a); both remain together in one selectable question. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use graphing software, then read the range from the plotted graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain the supplied exclusion using division by zero and recognise that cancelling the common factor does not define the original expression at zero.

questions.mappingNote: The explanation must account for the excluded input even though the fraction simplifies to one elsewhere. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Determine restrictions from the original denominator before cancelling common factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor quadratic denominators and exclude all original zeros despite cancellable factors, then recognise that x²+1 is always positive so the radical denominator imposes no restriction.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a)–(c) retain restrictions lost by cancellation. Part (d) checks that its denominator is defined and never zero. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Exclude zeros of each original denominator; a square root in a denominator requires a strictly positive radicand.

classification.difficultyReason: Intersect two opposing square-root restrictions to recognise a singleton domain, then evaluate its only permitted input to obtain the range; the hint supports a nongraphical approach.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded hint explicitly directs a solution without a graph. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Intersect the opposing radical restrictions, then evaluate the function at its only permitted input.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine radical and denominator restrictions with possible output values. The hardest part requires carrying the lower bound on x²+4 through a square root and reciprocal, identifying the attained maximum 1/2 while excluding zero.

questions.mappingNote: The shared instruction explicitly specifies the method. Parts (a)–(d) remain in the source two-column row order. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Reason about allowed inputs, possible denominator or radicand values, and resulting outputs without replacing the requested input/output reasoning with graphing.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the defining identities for even and odd functions and supply the missing expression in each statement.

questions.mappingNote: Each printed statement directly asks for the expression equal to f(-x). The statements on source page 12 supply the local context. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Complete the defining identities for even and odd functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the reflection axis for even functions and the centre of rotational symmetry for odd functions, with the statements supplying the response context.

questions.mappingNote: Each statement assesses one graphical consequence of the defining identities. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Identify the reflection axis of an even graph and the centre of rotational symmetry of an odd graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Inspect each supplied graph for y-axis reflection and origin rotational symmetry, selecting neither when both tests fail; no equation reconstruction or algebra is required.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess symmetry recognition. Fundamentals 2 on the same inspected source page supplies the relevant symmetry statements. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Use y-axis reflection symmetry for even functions and origin rotational symmetry for odd functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute -x into polynomial, exponential, radical and rational rules, simplify signs and powers, then compare with f(x) and -f(x); the rational neither case requires distinguishing two nonmatching identities.

questions.mappingNote: The shared instruction explicitly requires this substitution method. Fundamentals 1 on the inspected source page supplies the defining comparisons. All twelve rules were independently evaluated before comparison with answer-book page 11. Separate teaching evidence was unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Substitute -x for every occurrence of x, simplify, then compare with f(x) and -f(x).

classification.difficultyReason: Reflect each supplied branch in the y-axis, preserving heights, intercepts, endpoints and asymptotic behaviour; part (d) also maps the minimum from (-1,1) to (1,1).

questions.mappingNote: All four supplied graphs require the same even-function symmetry. The completed shapes were compared individually with Exercise 2C Q3(a–d) on answer PDF page 11.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were unavailable. The explicit even-function task is solved by reflection in the y-axis using f(-x)=f(x).

classification.difficultyReason: Apply origin symmetry to supplied branches, preserving extrema, intercepts, asymptotic behaviour and endpoint inclusion. The transformation is specified by the odd-function instruction.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses origin symmetry. Answer PDF page 11 contains Q4(a–b) at the lower left and Q4(c–d) as the continuation at the upper right.
questions.methodNote: Teaching pages were unavailable. The explicit odd-function task is solved by a half-turn about the origin using f(-x)=-f(x).

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute -x and use index laws to recognise the symmetric sum 2^x+2^(-x), then compare with the original function to establish evenness.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly requests an even-function proof for the displayed exponential function.
questions.methodNote: Substitute -x and simplify using index laws, then compare with f(x). No teaching pages were supplied.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute into the supplied sum and apply the two given even-function identities. The requested intermediate equality directly supports the subsequent classification and statement completion.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c form one shared-stem proof, classification and completion sequence. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Use the given even-function conditions when substituting -x into the supplied definition of h.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the relevant sum or product definition, apply the parity identities and simplify signs to compare h(-x) with h(x) or -h(x). The source explicitly supplies the proof strategy.

questions.mappingNote: Each printed statement maps to one proof response under the shared definition instruction. No separate teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Follow the explicit source instruction: define the relevant sum or product, simplify h(-x), and compare with h(x) or -h(x).

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the even and odd identities to differences and a quotient, tracking signs to judge three general claims. The preceding proofs supply the method, while the quotient requires distinguishing odd behaviour from the claimed even behaviour.

questions.mappingNote: The three printed statements map separately to inline True/False responses. No teaching pages were supplied.
questions.methodNote: Check parity by substitution. For the quotient, retain the nonzero-denominator condition; a counterexample establishes that the universal even-function claim is false.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the input/output relationship in composition, with initial letters supplied for both missing terms.

questions.mappingNote: The two clozes assess the input of the outside function and preserve the printed initial letters.
questions.methodNote: Preceding teaching evidence was unavailable. The visible task describes the inside-to-outside input/output relationship.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the inner and outer functions in two explicitly written compositions; no substitution or simplification is required.

questions.mappingNote: Each printed statement is retained as a distinct cloze part in its original vertical order.
questions.methodNote: Preceding teaching evidence was unavailable. The visible statements establish evaluation from the inside function to the outside function.

classification.difficultyReason: Form routine compositions, then work backwards from sqrt(x+8) to choose two applications of g followed by f, supported by the preceding result g(g(x))=x+8.

questions.mappingNote: The four distinct printed tasks retain their vertical order and shared radical and linear function definitions.
questions.methodNote: Preceding teaching evidence was unavailable. Solutions substitute the inside expression into the outside function. Repeated composition adds 4 twice before taking the square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Form each composition by direct substitution and simplify using linear algebra, index laws and a reciprocal-square-root identity; no unsignposted connection is required.

questions.mappingNote: Each source pair owns both composition responses. The source two-column order a, b, c, d is retained.
questions.methodNote: Preceding teaching evidence was unavailable. Each composition is formed by substitution, then simplified using ordinary algebra and index laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the rational function into both occurrences of its argument, combine the resulting denominator and simplify a compound fraction.

questions.mappingNote: The single response assesses rational self-composition. Necessary exclusions are retained after cancellation.
questions.methodNote: Preceding teaching evidence was unavailable. The solution substitutes the complete rational expression into both occurrences of the argument, combines the denominator, then simplifies.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied definition to form and simplify rational self-compositions, then decide whether each resulting expression equals x identically.

questions.mappingNote: The permanent definition remains once in the parent prompt. All four source functions remain separate response parts in a two-column grid.
questions.methodNote: The question supplies the test f(f(x))=x. Each solution forms and simplifies the self-composition, then applies that test.

classification.difficultyReason: Form the two compositions, identify the forbidden inputs from their denominators and the inner function, and compare the resulting domains; earlier parts scaffold the domain analysis.

questions.mappingNote: The two rational compositions and their different domain restrictions directly assess composite-function equations and domains.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the inner expression into the outer function; retain inner-domain restrictions and exclude zero denominators. Relevant teaching pages were not supplied.
